content.objective: Say what positioning is, and keep it apart from a real difference and from a value proposition.
content.explanation:
Positioning is how you want your market to think of you, next to the alternatives. It is a decision about being understood.

Three words sit close together here. A difference is what is actually different about your offer. Positioning is how you mean to be understood. A value proposition is why the customer you chose should care.

A café priced above its neighbours, with better beans and table service, is positioned as somewhere a bit special — what people often call premium. The price is part of the message, not only a number on the till.
content.whyMatters: You do not get to decide what customers think by saying it. They read it off what you charge, what you sell, and where you sell it.
steps: Say how you want the market to think of you.
List the choices a customer can actually see.
Check those choices say the same thing.

workedExample.prompt: A tea brand means to sit above Brand X in both price and how good people think it is. Today both sell at $4.50. The tea brand uses leaf from one estate; Brand X blends several. (Our scenario, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: We should say in our advertising that we are the premium option and that our tea is better quality.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I’d raise the price above Brand X. Sitting at the same price says we are the same kind of thing, whatever the advertising claims. The leaf from one estate gives us something the higher price can stand on.
workedExample.whyItWorks: It changes a signal the customer can see rather than only the wording. And the change is backed by a difference the situation already gives us.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A hotel says it is positioned as the quiet, restful option in town. Which of its choices contradicts that?
choices: The late-night bar it advertises on the front of the building
The blackout blinds fitted in every one of the bedrooms
The library lounge it keeps free of phones and screens
The garden it maintains at the back, away from the road
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: The late-night bar it advertises on the front of the building
guidedQuestion.hint: Which choice tells the customer something different?
guidedQuestion.explanation: A late-night bar advertised on the front of the building is the loudest thing about the place, which is not what a quiet, restful hotel is claiming to be. Blackout blinds, a screen-free lounge and a garden away from the road all point the same way as the claim.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Positioning is best described as:
choices: The list of features that make an offering different from the rest
How a business means its market to think of it against rivals
The benefit statement that a chosen customer is given to read
The amount a business charges when set against its nearest rivals
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: How a business means its market to think of it against rivals
practiceQuestions.hint: Three close words: different, understood, why care.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Features are the difference. The benefit statement is the value proposition. Price is one signal of a position, not the position itself.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A furniture maker means to sit below Northgate on price while staying the durable, repairable choice. Its chair is $220 and Northgate’s is $260. What should it do?
choices: Match Northgate at $260, so quality is not doubted
Cut to $150, to be clearly the cheaper option
Hold the chair at $220 where it already sits
Raise to $270, to sit just above Northgate
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Hold the chair at $220 where it already sits
practiceQuestions.hint: Does the current signal already say what you mean?
practiceQuestions.explanation: It is already below Northgate and not so far below that durability stops being believable. Matching at $260 loses the gap it wants, $270 puts it above Northgate when the intention was to stay below, and $150 says budget rather than durable.

masteryCheck.prompt: A business claims a premium position and advertises weekly discount coupons. What is the problem?
choices: Coupons are more expensive to run than other promotions
The signals contradict each other, so the claim is doubted
Premium businesses are not allowed to discount at all
Coupons reach the wrong age group for a premium product
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: The signals contradict each other, so the claim is doubted
masteryCheck.hint: Customers read the choices, not the claim.
masteryCheck.explanation: Nothing here says what coupons cost or who picks them up, and there is no rule against discounting. The problem is that the weekly discount says one thing while the claim says another.

teachingSections.heading: Your choices are the message
teachingSections.body:
Customers work out your position from what they can see: what you charge, what you stock, where you sell, how you look. Where a situation supports it, price is one of the clearest of those signals.

So a position has to be backed by choices that agree with it. A range — everything a business sells — can call itself clinical and top of its category. Run a permanent three-for-two on it (pay for two, take three) and you have told the customer two different things. The one they believe is usually the one with a price on it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Collapsing difference, positioning and value into “branding”.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: They answer three different questions, and a scenario is usually asking only one of them.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask which is wanted: what is different, how you mean to be understood, or why this customer should care.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating positioning as a slogan.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: A sentence in an advert cannot outvote the price on the shelf.
commonMistakes.fix: Change something the customer can see, then say it.

name: Identifying the Problem
description: Say what needs to change, using only the causes the scenario supplies.

lesson.title: Identifying the Problem
lesson.summary: Move from what the scenario says to what actually needs to change — without inventing a reason it never gave.

content.objective: Say what needs to change in one sentence, separate from the task, from what you can see, and from any solution.
content.explanation:
The problem is the thing that needs to change. It is not the task you were given, and not always the first thing you notice. Here is a scenario:

“You are an assistant manager at a bakery. The owner has asked to meet you. Customers have been picking up the wrong orders. The order slips are handwritten, and staff say orders get mixed up because the slips are hard to read. The owner wants you to recommend what the bakery should do.” (Our scenario, not an official one.)

What you notice is that customers get the wrong orders. What needs to change is that orders keep getting mixed up — and here the scenario gives a reason, because staff say the slips are hard to read.
content.whyMatters: A recommendation is only as good as the problem it answers. Aim at the wrong thing and everything after is wasted. Saying what needs to change is where this lesson stops; what to do about it comes next.
steps: What is going wrong? — the visible issue.
Who or what is affected?
What facts show it?
Does the scenario say why, or is the reason unknown?
What needs to change? — one sentence.

workedExample.prompt: You are an assistant at a gym. The manager has asked to meet you. Over the past two months fewer members have renewed their memberships. The gym has not changed its prices or its opening hours. The manager wants you to recommend what the gym should do. (Our scenario, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: The problem is that members are bored of the equipment, so we should buy new machines.
workedExample.strongAnswer: The task is to recommend what the gym should do. The scenario tells me fewer members renewed over the past two months, so it is renewals that are affected. The scenario does not say why, and it tells me price and opening hours have not changed, so I cannot point at either. My problem sentence: fewer members are renewing than two months ago. I would want to know why before saying what to change.
workedExample.whyItWorks: It says what needs to change without naming a reason the scenario never gave. It also uses what the scenario does rule out.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A scenario reads: “You are a supervisor at a cinema. Your manager has asked to meet you. Since a new snack counter opened, people waiting for snacks have been blocking the ticket queue. Your manager wants you to recommend how to fix the queue.” Which of these is the problem?
choices: You were asked to recommend a fix for the queue
People waiting for snacks are blocking the ticket queue
The cinema should move its snack counter elsewhere
The new snack counter is popular with customers
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: People waiting for snacks are blocking the ticket queue
guidedQuestion.hint: The task is what you were asked for. The problem is what needs to change.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The blocked queue is what needs to change. Being asked for a recommendation is the task, and moving the counter is something you could do about it. Nothing on the page says the counter is popular.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A scenario says only that a shop’s sales have fallen over the last three months. It gives no other information. Which problem statement does it support?
choices: Sales have fallen over the last three months
Sales fell because the prices are too high
Sales fell because a competitor opened nearby
Sales fell because the shop stopped advertising
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Sales have fallen over the last three months
practiceQuestions.hint: A scenario that says nothing about the cause has not given you one.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only one of these says what the scenario actually says. The others each add a reason the page never mentions, and any of them could be wrong without the scenario contradicting itself.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A scenario says a library’s evening study room is often full while its morning room sits empty. Which of these is a problem rather than a solution?
choices: The library should open another evening study room
The library should move chairs into the morning room
Evening study space runs out while mornings sit empty
The library should let students book a room ahead
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Evening study space runs out while mornings sit empty
practiceQuestions.hint: A solution is something to do. A problem is something that needs to change.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Three of these start with something the library should do, which makes them answers. Only one says what is actually going wrong.

masteryCheck.prompt: A scenario reads: “You are a receptionist at a vet clinic. The manager has asked to meet you. Appointments have been running late all week. The clinic books one appointment every ten minutes, and staff say most check-ups take longer than that.” Which problem statement does it support?
choices: Appointments have been running late all week
The clinic should book fewer appointments each day
The staff at the clinic are working too slowly
Appointments are booked closer together than check-ups take
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Appointments are booked closer together than check-ups take
masteryCheck.hint: This scenario does give you a reason — so you may use it.
masteryCheck.explanation: Ten-minute slots against check-ups that take longer is on the page, so it belongs in the problem. Running late is what you notice, booking fewer is something you could do, and nothing says anyone is working too slowly.

teachingSections.heading: The task is not the problem
teachingSections.body:
The task is what you were asked to produce. The problem is what needs to change. Two different sentences.

At the bakery the task is to recommend what the bakery should do. The problem is that orders are being mixed up.

“The problem is that I need to make a recommendation” names nothing that is wrong. It is the task wearing the word problem.

teachingSections.heading: What you notice is not always what needs changing
teachingSections.body:
The thing you can see is the symptom: complaints went up, orders are late, sales fell. It is real, it is where you start, and sometimes it is the whole story.

But it is not automatically the thing to fix. Not every scenario has something underneath: sometimes the visible issue is the issue. Look for what the facts support, not a hidden layer that has to be there.

Sometimes there is more. Customers getting the wrong orders is what happens; the handwritten slips are what staff say produces it.

teachingSections.heading: Only a cause the scenario gives you
teachingSections.body:
Sometimes the scenario tells you why. The bakery one does, because staff say the slips are hard to read. That is on the page, so you may use it.

Often it does not. If a scenario says only that sales fell, you do not know why. It might be price, a competitor, or the weather — possibilities, not facts.

Some facts are neither a reason nor ruled out. The scenario states them and never connects them to what is going wrong; leave those where they are.

A scenario silent about the cause has not given you one, and silence is not permission to pick whichever reason sounds best. “Sales have fallen over the last three months” beats a reason you made up.

teachingSections.heading: A solution is not a problem, and one sentence is enough
teachingSections.body:
“We should start a loyalty card” is something to do. “Customers rarely come back after a first visit” is something that needs to change. Only the second is a problem.

Write the problem as one sentence. Where the scenario gives a cause you may include it: staff say orders get mixed up because the handwritten slips are hard to read.

misconception.wrongModel: Every scenario hides a deeper cause, and my job is to dig it out.
misconception.whyItFails: It pushes you into inventing one when the scenario supplies none, and an invented cause is easier to knock down than none.
misconception.betterModel: Use the cause the scenario gives you. Where it gives none, say what needs to change and leave why open.

commonMistakes.mistake: Restating the task as the problem.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The task is what you were asked for, so it feels like the subject.
commonMistakes.fix: Check your sentence says what is wrong, not what you were asked to do.

commonMistakes.mistake: Naming a cause the scenario never gave.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: It is the easiest thing to challenge, and it takes your recommendation down with it.
commonMistakes.fix: If the scenario is silent, say what needs to change and stop.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a solution and calling it the problem.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: A solution answers a question you have not asked yet.
commonMistakes.fix: If your sentence contains “we should”, it is not the problem.

name: Business Reasoning
description: Test a recommendation for feasibility, benefit, measurement and cost before you say it.

lesson.title: Justifying Your Recommendation
lesson.summary: Turn an idea into a business decision: can this business do it, what would it gain, and what does it cost?

content.objective: Test a recommendation before you say it, and give the reason that makes it worth doing at this business.
content.explanation:
A recommendation is what you would do. Business reasoning is why it would work here.

Compare these two. “The shop should start a loyalty program.” Now the same idea with reasoning: “The shop could run a points scheme through the checkout system it already has. Setup costs almost nothing, regulars get a reason to come back, and the manager can check whether repeat visits go up.”

Both name the same action. Only the second says the shop can do it, what it gets back, and how anyone would know. That is the gap between an idea and a business decision.

The scenarios and figures here are ours. Yours come from your own scenario card: the sheet handed to you before a role-play — the practice meeting where you explain a recommendation to a judge. It sets the situation and its limits.
content.whyMatters: Judges hear plenty of ideas. Yours holds up when it survives the next question. Reasoning lets you answer “what will this cost us?” without inventing anything.
steps: Can we do it? Check the plan against every limit the card states.
Why would it help? Build the reason from a fact on the card.
How would we know? Name what you would watch and what it must reach.
What does it cost? Say what it uses up, and why the gain is worth it.

workedExample.prompt: You are the assistant manager of a bike shop. Repairs are booked three weeks out and the shop turns away about ten jobs a week. There is a spare bench, and one mechanic who works Saturdays only. The judge is playing the owner. (Our scenario, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: We should hire another mechanic. More repairs would mean more money coming in for the shop.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I’d move the Saturday mechanic to two weekday evenings. The bench is there, so the cost is his hours. That puts a second mechanic on the ten jobs we turn away. Saturdays lose their cover, so I’d try it for two months. The measure is the booking wait — three weeks now, and I want it under one week.
workedExample.whyItWorks: It fits what the shop has, and every fact about the shop comes off the card. It names the cost, says what the shop gives up, and picks one measure with a before.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which of these is business reasoning, rather than just an idea?
choices: Open a second shop downtown next year, starting early in the spring
Improve our customer service, because good service always matters to every business
Open Sundays, because the market next door runs then and draws customers
Launch a loyalty card for regulars at the start of next month
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Open Sundays, because the market next door runs then and draws customers
guidedQuestion.hint: Which one says why, using something about this business?
guidedQuestion.explanation: Three of these say what to do. Only one gives a reason drawn from this shop’s own situation — the market next door. Naming a season or a launch date makes a plan specific, not justified.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A shop has $400 and four staff-hours for a one-week promotion. Which plan is feasible?
choices: A window display and a flyer drop, using stock the shop already has
A radio ad the local station quotes at $900 for the week
A weekend sampling stand, staffed for six hours by two paid assistants
A printed catalog, quoted at $700 for the print run before any postage
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A window display and a flyer drop, using stock the shop already has
practiceQuestions.hint: Check the plan against both limits, not just the easier one.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Feasible means the business can actually carry it out with what it has. Only the display and flyers stay inside both the money and the hours. Two assistants for six hours is twelve staff-hours against four, and the two quoted prices are both above $400.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The judge asks what your plan will cost. The scenario gives no prices. What is the strongest answer?
choices: A confident figure, because a judge would rather hear a number than a hedge
A rough percentage of last year’s sales, worked out on the spot
Nothing about cost, since the scenario never supplied any prices at all
What the plan uses up in hours and materials, and how you’d price it
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: What the plan uses up in hours and materials, and how you’d price it
practiceQuestions.hint: Specific logic beats an invented number.
practiceQuestions.explanation: You can be exact about what a plan consumes without inventing a price for it. A made-up figure and a percentage worked out on the spot both fall apart under one follow-up, and saying nothing leaves the question unanswered.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A salon’s stated problem is that clients book once and never rebook. It starts offering a rebooking discount at checkout. Which measure shows whether that problem improved?
choices: Total sales for the month after the discount started
The share of clients who book a second appointment
How many clients say they liked being offered a discount
The number of discounts handed out at the checkout
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The share of clients who book a second appointment
practiceQuestions.hint: Measure the problem the scenario named.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The problem was clients not coming back, so the measure has to be clients coming back. Total sales move for other reasons, discounts handed out counts the action rather than the result, and an opinion is not the behaviour.

masteryCheck.prompt: A car wash is deciding whether to add a Saturday morning shift. Which reason best supports it?
choices: Weekend trade is growing across the car-wash sector as a whole
Customers always prefer having more times available to them
The site sits idle on Saturdays and the booking line logs refusals then
Rivals in the area open Saturdays, so this one must be losing that work
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: The site sits idle on Saturdays and the booking line logs refusals then
masteryCheck.hint: Which reason uses something the scenario states?
masteryCheck.explanation: Only one is built from this car wash: a site standing idle and refusals already logged. A sector trend, a claim about what customers always prefer, and an assumption about what rivals are taking would each be true of almost any business.

teachingSections.heading: Can we do it?
teachingSections.body:
Feasible does not mean good. It means the business can carry the plan out with what it has. Check it against every limit the card states, not just the easiest one. One staff-hour means one person’s work for one hour. A plan that fits the budget but needs six from a shop with three is not feasible.

Be careful what you count as a cost. A cost uses up money, time or capacity — the work a business can handle — enough to notice. Getting used to a new order form does not. Relabeling four hundred shelf tags does, because someone has to stand there and do it.

teachingSections.heading: Why would it help, and how would we know?
teachingSections.body:
Build the reason out of facts the scenario gave you. A reason that would be true of any business — “customers like convenience” — proves nothing about this one.

Then say how the business would know. A useful answer names the measure, what you would compare it to, and what would count as working. “Sales went up” is not enough, because sales move for all sorts of reasons.

Pick the measure that matches the problem the scenario named, and check the business can actually collect it. A shop with no customer accounts cannot track repeat visits.

teachingSections.heading: What does it cost?
teachingSections.body:
When you name a cost, put it beside what the business gets back. A price alone does not answer the question, and nor does a benefit with no price. Return on investment asks whether the benefit was worth what the business spent.

Most plans have a downside as well as an upside, and weighing the two is a tradeoff. Say the downside, then say why the gain still wins. “This costs more up front, but it pays back by spring” is a tradeoff. Naming only the good half is not.

misconception.wrongModel: If my idea is specific enough — what, who and when — it counts as business reasoning.
misconception.whyItFails: Specific is not the same as justified. A plan can name staffing and dates and still not say why this business should do it.
misconception.betterModel: The reasoning is the part that could change the owner’s mind. Take it away and you are left with an idea nobody has argued for.

commonMistakes.mistake: Inventing numbers the scenario never gave you.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: A made-up percentage falls apart under one follow-up, and the judge cannot check it.
commonMistakes.fix: Use the figures on the card. If you need one that is not there, say what you would look up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Backing a plan with a rule that would fit any business.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: “Faster is always better” and “every plan carries risk” are true everywhere, so they say nothing about this shop.
commonMistakes.fix: Point at something the scenario actually states.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the plan when the judge says it has been tried before.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Giving up answers nothing, and repeating the plan louder answers nothing either.
commonMistakes.fix: Offer a smaller or shorter version that would show whether it works this time.

name: Professional Communication
description: Present recommendations with executive clarity and confidence.

lesson.title: Sound like a business advisor
lesson.summary: Use concise structure, business vocabulary, and a confident close.

content.objective: Communicate with a clear opening, numbered points, and professional tone.
content.explanation: Professional communication is not fancy language. It means the judge can trust you because your answer is clear, calm, and business-focused.
content.whyMatters: DECA judges often score delivery and organization alongside the business idea.
steps: Open with the problem and goal.
Give two or three numbered recommendations.
Close with the expected result and how to measure it.

workedExample.prompt: Recommend a promotion plan.
workedExample.weakAnswer: I would do social media and stuff.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I recommend a two-part promotion plan: first, targeted short-form videos for local students; second, a referral offer measured by new customer sign-ups.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer is organized, specific, and measurable.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which opening sounds most professional?
choices: I have a two-part plan to improve repeat visits.
This is easy.
I guess maybe ads.
Whatever works.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: I have a two-part plan to improve repeat visits.
guidedQuestion.hint: Professional means clear and credible.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This opening frames the goal and structure.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many recommendation points are usually manageable?
choices: Two or three
Ten
None
Every idea possible
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Two or three
practiceQuestions.hint: Clear beats crowded.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two or three points allow enough depth without overload.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should the close include?
choices: Expected result and measurement
A new unrelated idea
An apology only
No conclusion
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Expected result and measurement
practiceQuestions.hint: Business judges like outcomes.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A measurable close shows business reasoning.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which phrase is strongest?
choices: Measured by referral sign-ups
It will be good
People like things
Trust me
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Measured by referral sign-ups
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for measurable business language.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This phrase gives the judge a concrete metric.

masteryCheck.prompt: What does executive clarity mean?
choices: Clear, organized, decision-ready communication
Longer words only
Speaking fast
No structure
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Clear, organized, decision-ready communication
masteryCheck.hint: Think useful to a decision-maker.
masteryCheck.explanation: Executive clarity helps the judge understand and trust the recommendation.

name: Reading Scenarios
description: Pull the role, audience, situation, task and limits out of a role-play scenario.

lesson.title: Reading the Scenario
lesson.summary: Work out who you are, who is listening, what happened, what you were asked to do, and which facts you actually have.

content.objective: Read a role-play scenario and name your role, audience, situation, task, and the facts and limits you were given.
content.explanation:
A scenario is the short business situation you are handed before a role-play. It tells you who you are, what is going on, and what you were asked to do. Here is one:

“You are the assistant manager of a coffee shop. Your store manager has asked to meet you. For the last three weeks the morning line has moved slowly, and some customers have left without ordering. Four staff work weekday mornings. The manager wants you to recommend what the shop should do.” (Our scenario, not an official one.)

Read it twice: once for what happened, once for what you were asked to do. Those are not the same thing.
content.whyMatters: Everything you say is built on this reading. A polished answer to the wrong task is still the wrong task, and an invented fact can be checked against the scenario.
steps: Who am I? — my role.
Who am I talking to? — my audience.
What happened? — the situation.
What am I asked to do? — the task.
What facts and limits do I have?

workedExample.prompt: You are a sales associate at a garden centre. The owner has asked to meet you. Since the plant display moved to the back last month, staff have noticed fewer people buying plants. The owner wants your recommendation about the display. (Our scenario, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Moving the display to the back killed plant sales, so I would put it back at the front and sales would recover.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I am a sales associate speaking to the owner. The situation is that staff have noticed fewer people buying plants since the display moved to the back last month. My task is to recommend what to do about the display. Nobody has told me why, or what the centre can spend, so I would treat the new position as something to check, not the proven cause.
workedExample.whyItWorks: It names what the scenario states and stops there. It keeps the move as something to check: the scenario says what staff noticed after it, never that it caused it.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A scenario reads: “You are a shift supervisor at a cinema. Your manager has asked to meet you. Since the new online booking system launched, the ticket-desk queue has been longer on Friday nights. Your manager wants you to recommend how to shorten it.” What is the task?
choices: The ticket-desk queue is longer on Friday nights
Recommend a way to shorten the Friday-night queue
Explain why the online booking system was launched
Decide whether the booking system should be kept
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Recommend a way to shorten the Friday-night queue
guidedQuestion.hint: The situation is what is happening. The task is what you were asked to do about it.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The longer queue is the situation — it is what is going on. The one thing the manager actually asks for is a recommendation about shortening it. Nothing in the scenario asks you to explain why the system was launched or to decide its future.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A scenario says the ticket-desk queue has been longer on Friday nights since a new online booking system launched. Which of these can you state as a fact?
choices: The booking system is what made the queue longer
The queue has been longer since the system launched
Most customers now book online instead of queueing
The ticket desk is short-staffed on Friday nights
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The queue has been longer since the system launched
practiceQuestions.hint: Since is not because.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The scenario says when the queue got longer, not what caused it. The other three each add something it never says — a cause, a booking habit, and a staffing level.

practiceQuestions.prompt: You are a sales assistant. Your scenario says nothing about a budget and nothing about hiring. Which recommendation stays inside the role you were given?
choices: I would hire two more assistants for Saturday mornings
I would approve a discount for everyone who waited
I would suggest we look at how shifts run
I would raise the store’s advertising budget this month
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: I would suggest we look at how shifts run
practiceQuestions.hint: Take the job you were given and nothing beyond it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Three of these hire someone or spend money, and nothing in the scenario says a sales assistant can do either. Suggesting the shop look at how its shifts run is something the role can offer.

masteryCheck.prompt: A scenario reads: “You are a receptionist at a dental practice. The practice has two treatment rooms. The manager has asked you to recommend how to fit in more appointments.” Which of these is a constraint on your answer?
choices: Two treatment rooms are available in the practice
You are the receptionist at the practice
The manager asked you for a recommendation
More appointments should be fitted in each day
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Two treatment rooms are available in the practice
masteryCheck.hint: A constraint is a limit your answer has to work within.
masteryCheck.explanation: Two rooms is the limit any plan has to fit inside. The other three name your role, your audience, and the thing you were asked to do — none of them limits what you can propose.

teachingSections.heading: Who you are, and who is listening
teachingSections.body:
Your role is the job the scenario hands you. In the coffee shop you are the assistant manager, talking to your store manager.

The role decides what you can offer. An assistant manager can recommend a change to the morning shift. They cannot promise to hire, unless the scenario says so.

The audience decides what is worth saying. A manager wants to know what to do and what it costs. How to speak to them is a separate lesson.

teachingSections.heading: What happened, and what you were asked to do
teachingSections.body:
The situation is what is going on. The task is what you were asked to do about it. Most scenarios contain both, and it is easy to miss one.

In the coffee shop, the situation is the slow morning line. The task is to recommend what the shop should do.

You can understand a situation perfectly and still answer the wrong question. Before planning, say the task back in your own words.

teachingSections.heading: The facts you were given, and the limits on your answer
teachingSections.body:
Facts are the details the scenario states: three weeks, four staff on weekday mornings, customers leaving without ordering.

A constraint is a limit your answer has to work within — a budget, a deadline, the staff available, a company policy. A fact becomes a constraint when your answer has to fit inside it, so four staff on weekday mornings is both.

The scenario says nothing about money, so you do not know what you can spend. Not knowing is different from knowing there is none.

Not every scenario carries every limit. A real scenario also lists performance indicators, the things the person scoring you is looking for. A separate lesson teaches what to do with them.

teachingSections.heading: A fact on the page is not a guess in your head
teachingSections.body:
This one costs the most marks. You may propose an action. You may not treat a guess as though it were already true.

The scenario never says why the line slowed, or whether you can hire. Say “we are losing customers because we are understaffed” and you have invented a cause. Say “I would check whether the morning shift is understaffed” and you have proposed a step.

Is claims a fact. Would proposes an action.

misconception.wrongModel: The scenario is background. The real work is the recommendation.
misconception.whyItFails: Guess the task and a strong answer answers a question nobody asked.
misconception.betterModel: The scenario is the brief. The rest of the round is built on reading it accurately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Answering the situation instead of the task.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The scenario describes a problem, so it feels like the question.
commonMistakes.fix: Find the sentence that asks you for something, and mark it first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Filling a gap with a number the scenario never gave.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: It is easy to catch, and it makes your other numbers look invented too.
commonMistakes.fix: Say what you would find out, instead of naming a figure.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking authority the role does not come with.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: A recommendation the role cannot make is not one the business can use.
commonMistakes.fix: Check the job title, then stay inside it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting to solve while you are still reading.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The first idea arrives before the facts, and you then read looking for agreement.
commonMistakes.fix: Finish the five questions first. The problem underneath is the next lesson.

name: Marketing
description: Explain what promotion is for, and judge whether audience, message and channel fit.

lesson.title: Telling Them About It
lesson.summary: Match the message to the people you chose, and use something that can actually reach them.

content.objective: Explain what promotion is for, and judge whether the audience, the message and the channel fit each other.
content.explanation:
Promotion is everything a business does to tell customers about an offer. It comes in several forms: advertising, short-term offers, selling in person, public relations, direct contact, and anything online.

Advertising is paid, and meant to reach a lot of people at once. A sales promotion is a short-term nudge to act now, like a two-week trial offer.

A community choir rehearses on Tuesday evenings in the town hall and wants new members who can get there. An advert in the local weekly paper reaches that area. A national campaign would reach far more people, almost none of whom could come on a Tuesday.
content.whyMatters: A message can be true, well written and completely wasted. Whether it works depends on who sees it and whether it says anything they wanted.
steps: Say who the message is for.
Ask what that group would actually want to hear.
Choose something that reaches them, not something popular.

workedExample.prompt: A garden centre wants its 8,000 existing loyalty-card customers to try a new houseplant range. Their email addresses are on the loyalty file. There is no paid-advertising budget this quarter, and the range launches in two weeks. (Our scenario, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Run a broad advertising campaign so that far more people in the area get to hear about the garden centre.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Email the loyalty list with a two-week in-store trial offer on the new range. We already have their addresses, so it costs nothing we do not have. These are people who know the centre. They only need a reason to come in for the new plants.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The audience is the one named, the channel already reaches them, and the message gives them something to do inside the launch window. The weak answer builds awareness among people who were not the target.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A Saturday football club for under-twelves needs players who live close enough to come every week. Which channel best fits?
choices: A post on a nationwide youth-sport discussion forum
A notice in the newsletters of nearby primary schools
A national radio advertisement broadcast on weekend mornings
A stall at a large sports expo in another region
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: A notice in the newsletters of nearby primary schools
guidedQuestion.hint: Which one reaches these people, in this place?
guidedQuestion.explanation: All four reach people interested in sport. Only one is limited to families living near enough to come every Saturday, which is what the club said it needs.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the difference between advertising and a sales promotion?
choices: Advertising is done online, and a sales promotion is done in a shop
Advertising is paid and reaches many; a promotion is a short-term nudge
Advertising is used by the large businesses, and promotions by smaller ones
Advertising is honest, while a sales promotion is really a marketing trick
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Advertising is paid and reaches many; a promotion is a short-term nudge
practiceQuestions.hint: One informs widely; the other asks for something now.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both can be online or offline and both are used by businesses of any size. What separates them is that a sales promotion is short-term and built around something to do now.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A pet shop’s target is owners of large dogs, who its records show buy one twelve-kilogram sack of food about every six weeks. It offers a loyalty stamp giving a free sack after twelve purchases. Why is that a weak promotion for this group?
choices: The reward is too far away for how often these owners buy
Loyalty schemes of this kind do not work well for pet shops
Twelve-kilogram sacks are the wrong size for the shop to sell
The shop should be advertising to new customers instead of these
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The reward is too far away for how often these owners buy
practiceQuestions.hint: Work the offer against how often they actually buy.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Buying every six weeks, twelve purchases is well over a year away. The offer asks for a wait these buyers will not feel. Nothing here says loyalty schemes or that sack size are wrong in general.

masteryCheck.prompt: Which promotion says something the customer would care about?
choices: Our new range is now available in all of our branches
We have been trading in this town for over forty years
Try the new range free for two weeks, in store
Our new range uses a redesigned packaging format
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Try the new range free for two weeks, in store
masteryCheck.hint: Does it give them something they wanted, and something to do?
masteryCheck.explanation: Three of these are facts about the business. One offers the customer something and says how to take it up, which is the part they can act on.

teachingSections.heading: Audience, message, channel
teachingSections.body:
A promotion has three parts and they all have to agree. Who is it for. What does it say. Where does it appear.

Pick the audience first, because it decides the other two. A message that means nothing to them is wasted, however well it is written. A channel they do not use cannot deliver it, however popular it is.

Keep it consistent, too. If the same customer meets three different versions of what you are, none of them lands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a channel because it is popular.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Reaching many people is not the same as reaching yours, and the ones you chose may not be there at all.
commonMistakes.fix: Start from where your group already is.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a promotion that just restates the product.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The customer already has to work out why any of it matters to them, which is the part you were meant to do.
commonMistakes.fix: Say what they get, and what to do about it.

name: Marketing
description: Name which marketing lever a decision belongs to, and tell price as a signal from price as arithmetic.

lesson.title: The Offering and Its Price
lesson.summary: Work out which of the four levers a decision is really about, and what a price is saying.

content.objective: Name which of the four marketing levers a decision belongs to, and tell a price question about meaning from a price question about money.
content.explanation:
Businesses have four controllable levers, usually called the four Ps: product, price, place and promotion. Product is what you provide. Price is what the customer pays. Place is how they get it. Promotion is how you tell them.

A sandwich shop sells only full-size baguettes, and customers say they want something smaller at lunch. Adding a half-size option changes the product — what the shop sells is now a different thing. Charging less for the same baguette would be a price decision, and neither is about how people get hold of it.

Some decisions touch two levers at once, so say which one the customer’s problem is about. And naming the lever is the easy half: choosing well inside it is the work, and the four Ps do not do that for you.
content.whyMatters: Getting the lever wrong sends the whole answer somewhere else. A queue problem answered with an advert is a promotion fix for a product fault.
steps: Say what the customer’s problem actually is.
Name which lever changes it: product, price, place or promotion.
Choose inside that lever, using what the situation gives you.

workedExample.prompt: A gym’s members say they want to train before work, and its records show most of them start work at nine. The gym opens at seven, when its first instructor arrives, though the building is accessible from six. It has an equipment area that needs no instructor. (Our scenario, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: We should advertise our early classes harder so more members know that we open at seven.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I’d let members use the equipment area unstaffed from six. What we sell does not include the hour they most want. That area needs no instructor, so the offering can change without waiting for staff.
workedExample.whyItWorks: It fixes the thing members named. The weak answer promotes an opening time that is still too late, which is a promotion answer to a product problem.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which of these is a promotion decision?
choices: Choosing to run a paid social-media advertising campaign
Choosing which shops will stock the new range
Choosing to add a smaller size to the product line
Choosing to sit ten percent above the nearest rival
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Choosing to run a paid social-media advertising campaign
guidedQuestion.hint: Which lever is being pulled: product, price, place or promotion?
guidedQuestion.explanation: Stocking is place, a new size is product, and sitting above a rival is price. Only one of these is about telling customers something.

practiceQuestions.prompt: “Place” in the four Ps means:
choices: The town or region a business decides to operate in
How and where the customer obtains the product
The shelf position a product is given in a shop
The country where the product is manufactured
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: How and where the customer obtains the product
practiceQuestions.hint: Place is about how it reaches the customer.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Place covers the path from seller to buyer — where they get it and how it gets there. A head-office location, a shelf position and a factory are all real things, and none of them is what place means here.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A judge asks what your price says about the product. Which answer is about price as a marketing decision?
choices: We sell it for $40 and it costs us $22, so a discount still pays
Sitting above the nearest rival tells buyers we mean to be the better one
A ten percent cut would need us to sell a lot more to make it back
Our costs went up this year, so the price had to follow them
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Sitting above the nearest rival tells buyers we mean to be the better one
practiceQuestions.hint: What does the price say, not what does it earn?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two of these work out whether the price pays for itself, and one says where the price came from. Only one answers what the price communicates, which is the marketing question that was asked.

masteryCheck.prompt: A gym sells only twelve-month memberships. Customers say they want to try it for a shorter period first. Which lever should change?
choices: Promotion — advertise the twelve-month membership harder
Price — reduce the cost of the twelve-month membership
Product — add a one-month membership to what is sold
Place — open a second branch on the other side of town
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Product — add a one-month membership to what is sold
masteryCheck.hint: What did the customers actually say was wrong?
masteryCheck.explanation: They did not say they had not heard of the gym, that it cost too much, or that it was hard to reach. They said the only thing on sale is the wrong length, so what is sold has to change.

teachingSections.heading: Two different price questions
teachingSections.body:
Price gets asked about in two ways, and they want different answers.

One is what the price says. Sitting above the nearest rival tells a customer you mean to be the better choice; sitting well below says something else. That is a marketing question.

The other is whether the price works — what it costs to make, what margin is left, whether a discount pays for itself. That is a money question, and it is not this lesson. Answering a “what does this price say” question with arithmetic misses what was asked.

commonMistakes.mistake: Answering a pricing question with margin arithmetic.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: It is a good answer to a question nobody asked, and it leaves the marketing question open.
commonMistakes.fix: Check whether you were asked what the price says or whether it pays.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the four Ps as a checklist that solves the problem.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Naming the category is not the same as choosing well inside it, and the four levers are not a complete answer to every situation.
commonMistakes.fix: Name the lever, then say what you would actually do with it.

name: Performance Indicators
description: Work out what a listed performance indicator asks, then demonstrate it in the scenario.

lesson.title: Understanding Performance Indicators
lesson.summary: Work out what an indicator asks for, show the business idea, and use it on your own scenario.

content.objective: Work out what a listed performance indicator is asking for, then show that business idea inside your own scenario.
content.explanation:
A performance indicator is a business skill the judge expects to see you use. They are listed on your scenario card — the sheet you are handed before a role-play, which sets the situation and says who you are. The wording is formal and textbook.

Here is one. Explain how businesses build customer loyalty. A weak answer: “Customer loyalty is really important for us.” A better answer: “Let’s give a free coffee on every sixth visit. Regulars get a reason to come back here instead of the shop over the road. And keeping a regular costs less than finding someone new.”

The second answer shows the idea working. The first only mentions it.

That gap is the whole skill. Saying the indicator’s words does not cover it. You cover it when the judge can hear you understand the idea, and see you use it here.

The indicators in this lesson are examples we wrote. Real ones come from your own card, worded differently.
content.whyMatters: Role-play events are commonly scored on how well you show each listed indicator. So a perfect answer to one cannot make up for two you never reached.
steps: Say the indicator back as a plain question.
Name its subject, and what it says about that subject.
Let the first word set the job.
Explain the idea, then use it on this scenario.
Say what you would watch to know it worked.

workedExample.prompt: You are the assistant manager of a small gym. Membership has fallen over the last three months. The judge plays the owner. A listed indicator reads: Explain the nature of customer retention. (Our example, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Customer retention is really important for a gym. We should focus on keeping our members happy.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Retention is keeping the members we already have, and it costs less than replacing them. Ours go quiet around month three. I’d have a trainer ring anyone who misses two weeks and offer a free session. Then I’d watch how many of them are still training three months later.
workedExample.whyItWorks: It says what retention is and why it saves money. Then it acts, in this gym. The check is about members staying — what the indicator names.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A listed indicator reads “Explain the nature of inventory control in a small shop.” What is the most useful first move?
choices: Say the indicator’s title out loud so the judge hears you cover it
Put it in your own words, as a question you could answer
Write out the textbook definition of inventory control from memory
Pick whichever business idea you already know best and use that one
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Put it in your own words, as a question you could answer
guidedQuestion.hint: You cannot show something you have not pinned down.
guidedQuestion.explanation: In plain words it becomes: what is stock costing this shop, and what should be on the shelf? Now there is something to answer. The other three start building before the indicator is understood.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A listed indicator begins with the word “Demonstrate.” What does that first word change?
choices: You should define the term carefully before using it anywhere else
You should name the indicator first, so the judge knows it is coming
You have to do the thing in the meeting, rather than describe it
You should leave it until last, once the rest of your plan is explained
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: You have to do the thing in the meeting, rather than describe it
practiceQuestions.hint: Some indicators ask for an action, not an idea.
practiceQuestions.explanation: “Demonstrate” asks for the thing itself, live. A perfect account of the procedure never lets the judge see it happen. Plan the moment instead: what will you actually do?

practiceQuestions.prompt: A listed indicator reads “Explain the nature of word-of-mouth promotion.” Which response does both halves of the job?
choices: What word of mouth does for a business, and what it does here
A careful definition of word of mouth, and of how it spreads between people
A decision to run a referral offer next month, stated clearly and confidently
A promise to think about word of mouth and report back after the meeting
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: What word of mouth does for a business, and what it does here
practiceQuestions.hint: The idea, and then this business.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A definition on its own is knowledge with nowhere to go. A decision on its own leaves the reasoning unsaid. Carrying the idea into this business does both jobs at once.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A listed indicator is about employee motivation. A student clearly explains what motivates the shop’s customers instead. Against that indicator, the response has:
choices: covered it, because the explanation was clear and well organised
covered it, because customers and staff both respond to motivation
explained the right subject, but at the wrong point in the meeting
explained the wrong subject, so the listed skill went unshown
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: explained the wrong subject, so the listed skill went unshown
practiceQuestions.hint: An indicator names a subject as well as a job.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The explanation is good, and it is about the wrong people. Adjacent topics are different skills, and only the unlisted one got shown.

masteryCheck.prompt: You move a café to smaller, more frequent milk deliveries. The listed indicator is about controlling stock costs. Which result best shows the judge it worked?
choices: How quickly the new supplier confirmed the change to smaller orders
Whether the staff found the new delivery routine easier to manage
How many deliveries the café ended up receiving in an average week
What the café spent on milk it threw away, before and after
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: What the café spent on milk it threw away, before and after
masteryCheck.hint: Measure the thing the indicator names.
masteryCheck.explanation: The indicator is about stock costs, so the check has to be about money spent on stock. Supplier speed, staff comfort and delivery counts all describe the change instead.

teachingSections.heading: What is it really asking?
teachingSections.body:
First, say it back as a plain question. Take “Explain the nature of staff morale in a shop.” In plain words: what makes staff here feel good or bad, and why does that matter? Now you can answer it. Many indicators start with “Explain the nature of…”, which just means: say what it is, and why it matters here.

Read the whole line, not just the topic. An indicator names a subject, and says something about it. One about employee motivation is not covered by explaining what motivates customers.

The first word sets the job. Explain and describe ask you to make the idea clear. Analyse asks you to break the situation up: which parts it affects, and how they knock into each other. Evaluate asks for a choice and the reasons behind it. Demonstrate asks you to do the thing, live.

teachingSections.heading: Show the idea, then use it here
teachingSections.body:
A full answer has two halves. First the idea: what the concept is, and why it matters. Then the use: what it means for this business, this problem, these limits. The same indicator asks for different things in different scenarios, so a general definition is not enough.

Then finish it. Say what you would watch to know it worked. Keep that check on the thing the indicator names. If the scenario gives you nothing to measure, say so rather than invent a number.

teachingSections.heading: Cover the whole list
teachingSections.body:
The judge is looking for every indicator on the list, whether or not their own questions reach it. If the conversation never reaches one, steer your answer there and show the idea working. While you plan, get one workable line on each before you make any of them longer.

Two indicators on one topic are still two jobs. “Describe the refund policy” and “Apply it to this customer’s request” ask for different things.

A budget or a staffing limit shapes how you show an indicator. A limit like that is not itself an indicator.

misconception.wrongModel: If I say the indicator out loud, or mention its topic, I have covered it.
misconception.whyItFails: Repeating the wording shows you can read. An answer that names every indicator and shows none has shown none.
misconception.betterModel: It is covered when someone who never saw your card could hear your answer and tell you understood the idea and used it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping at a definition when the indicator says demonstrate.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Describing how you would calm an unhappy customer is not calming the one the judge is playing.
commonMistakes.fix: When the verb asks for an action, plan the moment the judge watches.

commonMistakes.mistake: Doing brilliant work on something that was not listed.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Extra strength makes the meeting better. It still cannot stand in for a listed skill.
commonMistakes.fix: Reach every listed indicator first. Then give your remaining time to the weakest one.

name: Marketing
description: Tell a customer need, a market segment and a target market apart.

lesson.title: Who the Customer Is
lesson.summary: Work out what the customer is trying to get done, group the people trying to do it, and choose the group you can serve.

content.objective: Tell a customer need, a market segment and a target market apart, and say which one a situation is describing.
content.explanation:
Marketing starts with one question: who is this for? Three words get used for that, and they do not mean the same thing. A need is what the customer is trying to get done. A segment is a group of people trying to get the same thing done. A target market is the group the business chooses to build around.

A bike shop looks at who buys from it and finds three groups: commuters, weekend riders, and racers. That is segmenting — describing how the market divides. Choosing to build the shop around commuters is targeting. It is a decision, and it is why a commuter service package becomes the sensible next move.

Describing the groups is not a plan. “Our target market is anyone who might buy a bike” names the market and chooses nothing. A target you cannot be outside of is not a target.
content.whyMatters: Every later marketing decision points back at this one. Until you have chosen who you are for, you cannot tell whether an offer, a price or a channel fits.
steps: Say what the customer is trying to get done.
Group the people trying to get the same thing done.
Choose the group the business can actually serve.
Check the next decision follows from that choice.

workedExample.prompt: A bookshop wants one group to build its weekday campaign around. Its own records show most weekday sales are parents buying children’s books between two and four in the afternoon. Students come in mainly at weekends. (Our scenario, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: We should target readers. Everybody reads, so the campaign should go out to as many people as we can reach.
workedExample.strongAnswer: The records already point at one group: parents buying children’s books on weekday afternoons. I’d build the weekday campaign around them and time it before school pickup, because that is when the records say they are here. Students come at weekends, so they are a different campaign, not this one.
workedExample.whyItWorks: It picks a group the shop’s own records describe, rather than one it hopes exists. And the choice then decides the timing, instead of the timing being added afterwards.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A garden centre sorts its customers into weekend planters, allotment growers and landscapers. What has it done so far?
choices: Chosen a target market to build the season around
Described how its own market divides into different groups
Written a value proposition aimed at each of them
Decided which of the groups is the most profitable
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Described how its own market divides into different groups
guidedQuestion.hint: Describing the market and choosing inside it are different steps.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Sorting customers into groups is segmenting, and it describes the market. Choosing one to build around would be targeting, and nothing here says a choice has been made. What each group is worth is a different question again.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A gym’s members keep asking for more parking spaces. Asked why, they say they are trying to get in and out inside their lunch hour. What are they actually asking for?
choices: More parking spaces, added as soon as they can be built
A way to fit a workout into a lunch hour
A cheaper membership than the one they have now
Longer opening hours in the middle of the day
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A way to fit a workout into a lunch hour
practiceQuestions.hint: The request is not always the need.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The words name parking; the reason names the need. Once the need is a workout inside an hour, a quicker way through the changing rooms might answer it and more spaces might not. Nobody said price or opening hours was the problem.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A tutoring service has found four groups: 400 students wanting daytime courses, 150 adults wanting evening classes, 90 hobby learners wanting to drop in, and 60 candidates wanting weekend intensives. Its tutors work weekday evenings only. Which group is the sensible target?
choices: The 400 students who want intensive daytime courses
The 90 hobby learners who want to drop in any time
The 150 adult learners who want evening classes
The 60 candidates who want weekend intensives
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The 150 adult learners who want evening classes
practiceQuestions.hint: The biggest group is not automatically the reachable one.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only one group wants the service in the hours the tutors already work. Group size does not help when there is nobody there to teach them.

masteryCheck.prompt: Which of these is a target market?
choices: Anyone who might want to buy from us this year
People who like good service and fair prices
Office workers within a ten-minute walk, at lunchtime
Customers who are interested in what we sell
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Office workers within a ten-minute walk, at lunchtime
masteryCheck.hint: A target you cannot be outside of is not a target.
masteryCheck.explanation: Only one of these leaves anybody out. The others describe almost every possible customer, so they cannot help you decide what to offer or where to say it.

teachingSections.heading: Start from the need, not the product
teachingSections.body:
Ask what the customer is trying to get done. Meal-kit customers asking for a “quick mode” button are not really asking for a button. They are trying to get dinner made on a weeknight, and the useful answer is a set of fifteen-minute recipes.

A group is worth targeting when the business can actually serve it. The biggest group is not automatically the right one. If the tutors only work weekday evenings, four hundred students who want daytime courses cannot be reached, whatever the number says.

misconception.wrongModel: The target market is everyone who might possibly buy.
misconception.whyItFails: A target that excludes nobody gives you nothing to decide with. Every offer fits, every channel fits, and no plan is better than any other.
misconception.betterModel: A target market is a choice about where to concentrate. If nothing is left out, no choice has been made.

name: Marketing
description: Tell a difference from a value proposition, and test whether the difference matters.

lesson.title: Why They Would Choose You
lesson.summary: Turn a fact about your offer into the promise it makes to the customer you chose.

content.objective: Tell a difference from a value proposition, and test whether a difference actually matters to the customer you chose.
content.explanation:
A difference is something about your offer that is not true of the alternatives. A value proposition is the promise that difference makes to the customer you chose. They are not the same thing.

A bike repair shop returns every bike the same day. That is the difference. The value proposition is what it means to a commuter: your bike back the same day, ready for the ride to work tomorrow. One is a fact about the shop. The other is a reason to choose it.

Different is not the same as better. A shop could be the only one using purple boxes. True, checkable, and no reason for anyone to buy anything.
content.whyMatters: A feature on its own gives a customer nothing to decide with. What decides it is what the feature does for them, and whether that was something they were already trying to get.
steps: Name the difference.
Say what it gets the customer you chose.
Check that a competitor could not say the same sentence.

workedExample.prompt: A payroll software company sells to owners of businesses with fewer than five staff. Those owners say their worry is making a mistake on a tax filing. The software checks filings before they are submitted. (Our scenario, not an official one.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Our software includes an automatic pre-submission validation layer built into the filing workflow.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Your filings are checked before they are submitted, so mistakes get caught first. That is the thing these owners told us they were worried about, and it is what the check actually does for them.
workedExample.whyItWorks: It states the same fact in the customer’s terms. The weak version describes the software; the strong one answers the worry the owners named.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A window company’s frames are guaranteed for twenty-five years. Which is the value proposition?
choices: Our frames are guaranteed for a full twenty-five years
We use a reinforced core that resists warping over time
You will not be replacing these windows again for decades
Our frames are tested against a twenty-five year standard
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: You will not be replacing these windows again for decades
guidedQuestion.hint: Say what the difference gets the customer.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The others state a fact about the frames or about the guarantee. Only one says what that means for the person who has to live with them, which is the part they can decide with.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A bike shop lists four things no other local shop does. Which difference is useless to the customer?
choices: We are the only local shop with a green front door
We are the only local shop that opens before seven
We are the only local shop that repairs older frames
We are the only local shop that returns bikes the same day
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: We are the only local shop with a green front door
practiceQuestions.hint: A difference has to be one somebody would choose on.
practiceQuestions.explanation: All four are differences. Three of them change what the customer gets — earlier access, a repair nobody else does, a shorter wait. The colour of the door changes nothing they were trying to do.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two versions of the same printer cartridge cost the same. One can be collected today from a store twenty-five minutes away; the other arrives by post in four days. A customer whose printer is out of ink now would take:
choices: The posted version, since waiting avoids the trip
Either one, because the price is the same either way
The store version, collected today rather than posted
Neither, until a cheaper option can be found
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The store version, collected today rather than posted
practiceQuestions.hint: Value is the benefit set against what it costs to get it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The price is identical, so price cannot decide it. What differs is the wait, and this customer needs ink now — so the trip buys something they actually want.

masteryCheck.prompt: A mobile dog groomer comes to the owner’s door, so an anxious dog never travels. Which sentence is the value proposition?
choices: We operate a fully equipped grooming van with onboard water
No car, no waiting room. We groom at your door.
We are a mobile grooming service covering the whole county
Our groomers are trained to work with nervous animals
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: No car, no waiting room. We groom at your door.
masteryCheck.hint: Which one names what the owner gets?
masteryCheck.explanation: The others describe the van, the coverage and the training. Only one says what changes for the owner and the dog, which is the reason to choose it.

teachingSections.heading: Turn the feature into the promise
teachingSections.body:
Say the difference, then say what it gets the customer. Paper that does not bleed through is a feature. Both sides of every page stay usable is the promise.

A value proposition that would fit any competitor is not one. If a rival could put their name on your sentence and it would still be true, you have described the category rather than your own offer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Listing features and calling it value.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: A feature is a fact about the product. It becomes value only when someone says what it does for the customer.
commonMistakes.fix: After each feature, say “which means…” and finish the sentence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Claiming a difference the situation does not support.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: If nothing in front of you says you are the only one, saying so is a guess the customer can check.
commonMistakes.fix: Point at the difference the situation actually gives you.

name: Healthcare Ethics
description: Make responsible choices using safety, privacy, and respect.

lesson.title: Reason through healthcare ethics
lesson.summary: Use privacy, consent, safety, and fairness to evaluate scenarios.

content.objective: Use ethical principles to choose a safe and respectful response.
content.explanation: Healthcare ethics often involves balancing values like privacy, patient choice, safety, and professional responsibility.
content.whyMatters: HOSA scenarios may test what you do when the easy answer is not the most responsible answer.
steps: Identify the people affected.
Name the ethical issue.
Choose the safest professional action.
Explain why it respects the patient.

workedExample.prompt: A friend asks about a patient's condition.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Tell them if they promise not to share.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I cannot share private patient information. I would direct them to the proper contact process and protect confidentiality.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer protects privacy and gives a professional next step.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which principle is involved when protecting patient information?
choices: Privacy
Marketing
Weighing
Pricing
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Privacy
guidedQuestion.hint: Think about information access.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Patient information should be protected unless sharing is authorized.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should you do with private patient information?
choices: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
Tell friends
Post it
Guess publicly
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
practiceQuestions.hint: Privacy rules matter.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Professional ethics requires protecting patient information.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is an ethical response?
choices: Respect patient dignity
Ignore consent
Embarrass the patient
Skip safety
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Respect patient dignity
practiceQuestions.hint: Ethics centers people.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Respecting dignity supports professional care.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why explain your ethical choice?
choices: To show reasoning and professionalism
To make it longer only
To avoid action
To confuse the judge
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To show reasoning and professionalism
practiceQuestions.hint: Judges need to see your decision process.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Explaining the principle makes the answer stronger.

masteryCheck.prompt: A scenario involves risk of harm. What principle becomes urgent?
choices: Safety
Advertising
Speaker rank
Budget
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Safety
masteryCheck.hint: Health scenarios prioritize harm reduction.
masteryCheck.explanation: Safety is central when someone could be harmed.

name: Medical Terminology Basics
description: Break clinical words into roots, prefixes, and suffixes.

lesson.title: Decode medical terms
lesson.summary: Use word parts to understand unfamiliar health terms.

content.objective: Break medical terms into word parts and explain them accurately.
content.explanation: Many medical terms are built from prefixes, roots, and suffixes. If you can identify parts, you can understand unfamiliar terms more safely.
content.whyMatters: HOSA events reward accurate health science language. Terminology also helps you communicate clearly with patients and judges.
steps: Find the prefix.
Find the root.
Find the suffix.
Put the meaning together and check context.

workedExample.prompt: Tachycardia
workedExample.weakAnswer: A heart problem.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Tachy means fast and cardia relates to the heart, so tachycardia means a fast heart rate.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer uses word parts and avoids vague guessing.

guidedQuestion.prompt: In tachycardia, what does tachy mean?
choices: Fast
Slow
Lung
Skin
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Fast
guidedQuestion.hint: Think of tachometer: speed.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Tachy means fast.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What does cardi relate to?
choices: Heart
Liver
Bone
Skin
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Heart
practiceQuestions.hint: Cardiology studies the heart.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cardi/cardio refers to the heart.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why use word parts?
choices: To infer meaning safely
To diagnose without context
To avoid communication
To skip definitions
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To infer meaning safely
practiceQuestions.hint: Word parts are clues, not the whole clinical picture.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Word parts help decode terms while still respecting context.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is most precise?
choices: Tachycardia means fast heart rate
Tachycardia is bad stuff
Tachycardia is always fatal
Tachycardia means slow breathing
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Tachycardia means fast heart rate
practiceQuestions.hint: Avoid exaggeration.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This answer is accurate and appropriately limited.

masteryCheck.prompt: What does hypo usually mean?
choices: Low or under
High
Heart
Bone
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Low or under
masteryCheck.hint: Hypo means below.
masteryCheck.explanation: Hypo often means low, under, or deficient.

name: Patient Communication
description: Explain health information clearly, respectfully, and safely.

lesson.title: Communicate with patients clearly
lesson.summary: Use empathy, plain language, and confirmation checks.

content.objective: Explain health information in plain language and confirm understanding.
content.explanation: Patient communication combines accuracy and empathy. A strong response avoids jargon, listens to concerns, and checks understanding.
content.whyMatters: In healthcare, communication affects safety. Patients need to understand next steps, risks, and when to ask for help.
steps: Acknowledge the concern.
Explain in plain language.
Give the next step.
Ask a teach-back question.

workedExample.prompt: A patient is nervous about a blood pressure reading.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Your systolic is elevated; just calm down.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I understand this number can feel stressful. Blood pressure can change for many reasons, so we will recheck it and share it with the provider. Can you tell me what step we are taking next?
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer is empathetic, clear, and checks understanding.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which response best uses plain language?
choices: We will recheck your blood pressure and talk with the provider.
Your systolic parameter requires clinical correlation.
Do not worry about it.
This is definitely a diagnosis.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: We will recheck your blood pressure and talk with the provider.
guidedQuestion.hint: Plain language is accurate and understandable.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This response avoids jargon and gives a safe next step.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is teach-back?
choices: Asking the patient to explain the next step in their own words
Repeating jargon faster
Ignoring questions
Giving a diagnosis
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Asking the patient to explain the next step in their own words
practiceQuestions.hint: It checks understanding.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Teach-back helps confirm the patient understands.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which tone is best?
choices: Calm and respectful
Dismissive
Sarcastic
Rushed
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Calm and respectful
practiceQuestions.hint: Healthcare communication needs trust.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A calm tone supports professionalism and patient safety.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why avoid jargon?
choices: Patients may not understand it
It is always illegal
It makes answers shorter
It replaces accuracy
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Patients may not understand it
practiceQuestions.hint: Communication is about understanding.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Plain language improves comprehension without sacrificing accuracy.

masteryCheck.prompt: A patient says they are confused. What should you do?
choices: Pause and explain again in simpler language
Move on immediately
Use more abbreviations
Ignore the concern
